# Seeing Relationships {#sec-seeing-relationships}

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
source("_console.R")
```

Modules 1 to 6 were about one variable at a time: how is yield distributed, what is the
mean, what is the spread.  This module is about pairs of variables: does yield change with
fertilizer, does price move with quality, do two crops rise and fall together.

Almost every interesting question in data analysis is a question about a relationship.  The
rest of the course is, in one way or another, about formalizing these questions.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Read a scatter plot before computing anything from it.
2. Say whether a relationship looks linear, curved, or absent.
3. Spot outliers and explain why one point can move a fitted line.
4. Recognize spread that grows across the plot, and hidden subgroups.
:::

## Look First {#sec-look-first}

You met the scatter plot in @sec-graphing-principles: one variable on each axis, a point for
every observation.  Here we use it for a different purpose.  There it was a way to *show* a
relationship to a reader.  Now it is a way to *find out* what the relationship is, before you
put a number on it.

The order matters.  Every summary in this module -- the correlation, the fitted line -- is a
single number standing in for a whole cloud of points.  Each one assumes something about the
shape of that cloud, and each one will hand you an answer whether or not the assumption holds.
The plot is how you check.

The dataset for this module is [`canola_trial.csv`](practice/data/canola_trial.csv).
Download it into your project's `data/` folder and load it:

```r
library(tidyverse)

trial <- read_csv("data/canola_trial.csv")
```

It has 120 canola fields, each with a nitrogen rate (`fertilizer_kg_ha`), growing-season
rainfall (`rainfall_mm`), the `variety` grown, and the `yield_bu_acre` harvested.

The workbook below opens to the **Scatter plots** sheet. Its point cloud is linked to the same 120 rows used in the R examples.

## Four Things to Look For {#sec-what-to-look-for}

### Is it a line, or a curve? {.unnumbered}

The methods in this module fit straight lines.  If the cloud bends, a straight line will
still be fitted, and it will still report a slope, and the slope will be misleading.

Curvature is common in agronomy.  Fertilizer response is the standard case: the first
50 kg/ha of nitrogen buys a lot of yield, the next 50 buys less, and past some point more
nitrogen does nothing.  That is a curve, and forcing a line through it understates the effect
at low rates and overstates it at high ones.

### Is one point running the show? {.unnumbered}

A single observation far from the rest can pull a fitted line a long way, particularly if it
sits at the far left or right of the plot.  A point out at the edge has leverage: it is a long
way from the centre of the data, so tilting the line toward it costs little elsewhere.

When you see one, find out what it is before you decide what to do.  A field that yielded
9 bu/ac because it was hailed out is a real observation, but it is not telling you about the
fertilizer response, and it does not belong in a regression that is meant to.  A yield of
340 bu/ac is a data-entry error.  Neither should be dropped silently -- say what you removed
and why.

### Does the spread stay the same? {.unnumbered}

Look at how tightly the points hug the trend at the left of the plot, and compare it with the
right.  If the scatter fans out -- tight at low values, wide at high ones -- the relationship
is less predictable at one end than the other.

The fitted line can still be a reasonable summary.  What breaks is the uncertainty around it,
which is calculated assuming the scatter is even.  We will not do anything about that in this
module; Modules 11 to 13 are where uncertainty gets treated properly.  For now, notice it and
say so.

### Is the cloud actually two clouds? {.unnumbered}

Sometimes what looks like one relationship is two groups sitting in different places.  Two
varieties with different yield potential, two soil zones, two years with different weather.
Colour the points by a third variable and the structure appears:

```r
ggplot(trial, aes(x = fertilizer_kg_ha, y = yield_bu_acre, colour = variety)) +
  geom_point()
```

This matters more than it looks.  A relationship computed across mixed groups can be quite
different from the relationship within each one -- occasionally it even points the other way.
That is a real phenomenon with a name, Simpson's paradox, and the multiple regression in
@sec-multiple-regression is one way of dealing with it.

## Anscombe's Quartet {#sec-anscombe}

The argument for plotting first has a famous demonstration.  Frank Anscombe built four small
datasets that share almost every summary statistic: the same means, the same standard
deviations, the same correlation, the same fitted line.  Plotted, they look nothing alike --
one is a tidy linear relationship, one is a clean curve, one is a perfect line with a single
outlier dragging it, and one is a vertical stack with one point off to the side.

It ships with R, so you can see it yourself:

```r
anscombe
```

Four numbers agreed on four datasets that have nothing in common.  Any of the summaries in
this module can be computed on data it has no business describing.  Plot first.
